EMPIRICAL RESEARCH PLAN  

------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy  
------------------------------------------------------------
Primary strategy: staggered Difference-in-Differences (DID) with an event-study (dynamic DID) specification.

Why appropriate?  
• Two states (NY, PA) adopt mandatory public CABG report cards at known but different dates (Dec-1990, Nov-1992).  
• All other states remain untreated through 1994.  
• Large multi-year patient-level panel allows pre- and post-period observation for treated and control states.  
• Outcomes are measured at the patient level but treatment is imposed exogenously by a state-level regulatory shock, satisfying the “as-good-as-random” timing condition conditional on trends.

The event-study extension allows visual and formal pre-trend testing and heterogeneous dynamic effect estimation (Barnett-Goodman / Sun-Abraham estimator to avoid bias with staggered timing).

------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control  
------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
Treat_st  = 1 if patient i is treated in state-year t where:  
 • state = New York & admission_date ≥ 1 Jan 1991 (first full calendar year after the Dec-1990 release)  
 • state = Pennsylvania & admission_date ≥ 1 Jan 1993 (first full calendar year after the Nov-1992 release)

Control group  
All Medicare AMI or CABG admissions in the 48 remaining states and D.C. that did NOT publish similarly detailed CABG report cards before 1995. (Drop CA & WI, which had rudimentary discharge-abstract systems, in robustness.)

Treatment timing  
NY: policy_year = 1991 onward  
PA: policy_year = 1993 onward  

No running variable → not an RDD.

Unit of analysis  
Patient admission spell; cluster standard errors at the state or hospital level.

------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Parallel Trends: In the absence of report cards, patient sorting, procedure use, expenditures, and mortality in NY & PA would have evolved like those in non-adopting states.  
• Plausibility: Pre-1990 (NY) and pre-1992 (PA) data give 3–5 years to assess.  

A2. Stable Composition: No systematic change in the age-65+ Medicare population unrelated to the policy but correlated with outcomes.  
• Plausibility: Medicare eligibility rules stable; we control for demographics and baseline illness proxies.  

A3. No Spillovers/Contamination: Publication in NY/PA does not directly alter provider behavior or patient sorting in control states.  
• Plausibility: Some spillovers near borders possible; addressed in robustness.  

A4. Exogeneity of Timing: Adoption dates determined by state political process, unlikely correlated with short-run outcome shocks.  
• Plausibility: Both states decided years earlier; no coincident Medicare rules affecting only those states.  

A5. No Differential Coding Changes: If NY/PA altered diagnostic coding intensity differently from controls, risk adjustment may be biased.  
• Plausibility: Use raw clinical outcomes (mortality) that are hard to up-code; risk-score measures used only as controls.

------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation  
------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Differential pre-trends (violating A1).  
• Mitigation:  Event-study coefficients for −5…−1 years; include state-specific linear trends; re-weight by pre-period covariate distributions (Abadie IPW).  

T2. Patient or provider migration across state lines (spillovers).  
• Mitigation:  Drop border-county admissions in main spec; run robustness including them to bound effects.  Test whether treated-state patients increasingly receive surgery out-of-state.

T3. Concurrent state-specific health-policy shocks (e.g., NY certificate-of-need revisions).  
• Mitigation:  Collect major state legislation in 1987-94 and include dummies; include hospital fixed effects in hospital-level regressions; or difference-in-difference-in-differences (DDD) using non-cardiac surgical admissions within the same states as an additional control outcome.

------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline  
------------------------------------------------------------
```r
#-----------------------------------------------------------
# 0. Packages
#-----------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)   # fast data wrangling
library(fixest)       # fast feols DID / event study
library(did2s)        # Sun–Abraham implementation
library(ggplot2)

#-----------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Load & Merge
#-----------------------------------------------------------
claims <- fread("medicare_claims_87_94.csv")           # AMI & CABG spells
aha    <- fread("aha_hospital_87_94.csv")

# merge hospital characteristics
setkey(claims, provider_id, year)
setkey(aha, provider_id, year)
claims <- aha[claims]     # left join

#-----------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Construct Variables
#-----------------------------------------------------------
# policy year by state
claims[, policy_year := fifelse(state=="NY", 1991,
                         fifelse(state=="PA", 1993, 9999))]

claims[, treat := as.integer(year >= policy_year)]
claims[, ever_treat := as.integer(state %in% c("NY","PA"))]

# Event time (relative to first treated year)
claims[, event_time := year - policy_year]
# Collapse event times beyond window
claims[event_time < -5, event_time := -5]
claims[event_time >  5, event_time :=  5]

# Outcomes
claims[, died_1yr   := as.integer(death_date <= admission_date + 365)]
claims[, any_cabg_yr:= as.integer(cabg_date <= admission_date + 365)]
claims[, spend_1yr  := total_hosp_spend_1yr]          # already inflation-adj?

# Controls
controls <- c("age","female","black","rural_resident",
              "lag_inpt_days","lag_inpt_spend")

#-----------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Main DID Specification
#-----------------------------------------------------------
did_main <- feols(died_1yr ~ treat + i(year) + i(state) + 
                    age + female + black + rural_resident +
                    lag_inpt_days + lag_inpt_spend,
                  data = claims,
                  cluster = ~state)

summary(did_main)

#-----------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Event-Study (Sun & Abraham)
#-----------------------------------------------------------
es_sa <- feols(died_1yr ~ sunab(policy_year, year) + 
                 age + female + black + rural_resident +
                 lag_inpt_days + lag_inpt_spend,
               data = claims[year %between% c(1987,1994)],
               cluster = ~state)

iplot(es_sa); abline(v=0,lty=2)  # quick visual check

#-----------------------------------------------------------
# 5. Robustness: Drop border counties within 50 miles
#-----------------------------------------------------------
# Suppose border_flag constructed externally
did_rob <- feols(died_1yr ~ treat + i(year) + i(state) + controls,
                 data = claims[border50==0],
                 cluster=~state)
summary(did_rob)
```

------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results (Priors)  
------------------------------------------------------------
• Quantity/Incidence of CABG: likely falls for high-risk (sicker) patients in treated states (provider risk-selection), small or no change for low-risk.  
• Expenditures: ambiguous — fewer surgeries for sick may lower average spending, but increased angioplasty use could offset. My prior: –3% to –5% spending among high-risk patients.  
• Mortality:  
 – Low-risk patients: modest reduction (≈ −0.5 to −1.0 pp one-year mortality, baseline ≈ 5-6 %).  
 – High-risk patients: possible rise (+0.5 pp) if they are shunned or delayed.  
Net social welfare: probably positive for average patient but negative for the sickest quintile.

------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID)  
(C1-C5 from Angrist & Pischke / Roth)  
------------------------------------------------------------
C1: Pre-treatment parallel trends visually and statistically supported ……… 0.8  
C2: No simultaneity or reverse causality (policy predetermined) ……………… 1  
C3: No interfering spillovers to controls ……………………………………… 0.5  
C4: Stable composition of treated and control units …………………………… 0.8  
C5: Correctly specified standard errors / clustering ………………………… 1  

(Scale 1 = clearly satisfied, 0 = questionable; decimals allowed.)

Overall, the design is credible but hinges on demonstrating parallel trends and minimal spillovers, both of which will be documented with the event-study and robustness exercises.
